notes: I compared the cards and judged them against the owner's words: line art that draws structure, a real halo kept where the phosphor is, grounded companion colours, and change that shows across the content. r20-mut-3 and r19-mut-2 carry the rail language through every page and keep the light where it means something. The two are close, and r20-mut-3 wins by a little because its type and light are more consistent with the CRT. r20-mut-1 is sound but nearer to today's page. r20-mut-2 changes the type most but is the most contrasty. The brown of r17-wild-1 is the owner's known aversion. The files stage/candidates-short.md and stage/table.md were missing, so I judged from the cards alone and did not use the measures or the designers' own notes.

scores.why: Calm and recognisably phosphor with a real halo, but everything is one monochrome green-on-black pass and the pages are plain cards; the owner's 'nearly identical' test starts here.

Fine rails and keyed section heads run through every page (Signal Box lineage), cyan, violet and amber stay low-chroma and bounce off the green. The bloom on the lit key word, the monitors and the floor-grid lamp bring the tube's light back where it belongs. The condensed headings and numbered tabs change the page's type, not only its colour. Risk: many lines and glows in places.

The rail and track language is the most legible: To do's lamps and 'was due' margin, Chat hanging from Vera, Status rails. The lit 'mind' has a good halo and the gauge and week dial are lovely. The serif headings and counts are a real typesetting gain. Faults: the full-width green Add button on To do is glare, and the serif sits a little off the CRT feel.

Grounded and coherent: a left dock of monitor, pager and status on every page, a typed prompt on the glass, a bar-scope readout and even rows. CRT soul is strong and the colours are restrained. It reads as a close cousin of today's structure, so less change in the content than the leaders.

The boldest typographic change: giant condensed numbered headings, a ledger rail and hatched swatches that alter the content of every page. But the huge white-and-green MIND and heavy headings are more contrasty than the owner asked for, and the tube's soft glow is mostly confined to the monitor.

A true page-wide change (blueprint grid, sheet title blocks, scalloped chat bubbles) with grounded teal. But the blueprint conceit pushes toward 'more blue than necessary' and away from the green-screen soul, and the grid adds noise behind everything.

Tidy, grounded and well made, with a nice Coming up track and monitor dock. It is the closest to today's page, which the owner has said reads as nearly identical, and it is the plainest of the finalists.

The pixel face and pewter monitor are a committed retro identity and the rail down the page is a good idea. The dotted heading bars and pixel type cost readability and polish, and the effect feels gimmicky rather than refined.
The wood-brown bars, rivets and condensed caps are exactly the warm brown the owner rejected as off-motif. The glow is faint and the dense three-column cards are heavy.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the rails, keyed section heads and the glow on the key word, monitors and floor lamp. Thin the extra lines on Chat and Ideas and soften the grid floor so only the lit parts glow.
Keep the rails, the lit 'mind', the gauge and the week dial. Replace the full-width green Add bar on To do with a compact primary button, and test a more machine-like heading face beside the serif.

Keep the typed prompt on the glass, the scope readout and the even dock. Add the rail and key language of the leaders to the page body, and vary the section heads so the pages differ more from today's.
Keep the condensed numbered index, ledger rail and hatched swatches. Calm the headline size and brightness, drop the page-wide white, and extend a halo from the monitor to the lit key word.
Keep the sheet title blocks, the NOW scale and the lit scale. Fade the grid to near-invisible, reduce the teal wash toward neutral green-black, and bring back the bloom on the glass.
Keep the dock and the Coming up track. Make the type and rhythm of the page body (headings, counts, row spacing) differ from today's so the change is seen across the content.
Keep the left rail with NOW and the pewter monitor. Drop the pixel face for body headings, remove the dotted bar fills in the section heads, and keep the pixel type for the machine's words only.
Keep the loop line under titles and the tiny lamps. Replace the brown bars and wood panels with the green-black neutral, and lighten the dense cards.

notes: The top two put the CRT in the content: the question and the figures are drawn on the glass, and the rest stays grounded. That is the lit-where-attention-belongs result. The lower four change the page more through type and materials than through phosphor, and the giant bloomed word in r20-mut-2 is glare, not afterglow. Figures drawn on glass (gauge, plot, radar) are the best idea in the field, and r20-mut-1 does the most with it.

scores.why: The original tube light is all there (halos, bloom, scanlines, lit monitors), but the page is nearly one green on black, so it is lit without much variation. It is the yardstick for what we are keeping.

Puts the most of the page on glass. The question is typed as a lit line on a green screen with a LISTENING status. Next up is a plotted bar scope, the radar has numbered points, and Status has a limit-flagged gauge. The glow is concentrated on screens and the page around them is calm and grounded, so the phosphor feels real and changes whole pages.

The desk terminal holds Vera, the next plan and the typed question on one real CRT. Status carries a glass gauge and the lists are quiet ledgers. It is very convincing as a monitor and calm elsewhere, but off the glass it is closer to today than mut-1.

Keeps the monitors and a bloomed MIND, and adds lit rails, a NOW lamp, a perspective grid floor under the glass and an UP lamp in the foot. Condensed type with keyed numerals gives a clear system. The grid lines are slightly busy, and it reads less as a green screen than as a console.

Pixel type, beige-cased monitors with slotted bases and a lit NOW rail give strong 1980s personality across every page. The monitors are the most real hardware here. The pixel face on body headings tips toward kitsch and costs some calm.

The scan-lined, haloed word 'mind', the lit rail node, the serif heading with a glowing count and the lamp-keyed filters are tasteful and lively. The page is calm and clearly different from today. The glass is today's, and the scanline word reads a little noisy.

Huge condensed type with a giant green MIND is a bold typographic move and shows across all pages. But the solid bloomed block is glare on the page, not light where attention belongs. The tube is only a sticker on an editorial layout.

The glowing MIND on a cream wide headline, with the NOW line and ticks, is lit well. The teal blueprint grid and sheet labels pull the page to another theme: it is no longer a green screen, and its grid is a wash across the page.

Wood rails, bronze screws and condensed caps are grounded and material, and the monitors sit well in it. But the page glow is low and the soul is hardware, not phosphor. Little lit besides the monitors, so it is the least alive here.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the glass-typed question, the plotted scope and the gauge. Let the typed headline's glow be a little less wide, and make the bar plot's axes a touch brighter so it reads at a glance.
Keep the all-in-one terminal. Carry more of the glass into a second figure (a plotted trace) and vary the type below it, so pages away from the monitor change more than the lists.
Keep the lamp rails, the NOW marker and the keyed nav. Thin or fade the background grid so it does not wash the page, and keep the glow on MIND and the screens.
Keep the beige-cased monitors, the NOW rail and the pixel digits. Return headings and chat names to the sans so the pixel face stays on the glass and the date numerals.
Keep the lit rail, the serif figure and the lamp-keyed filters. Calm the scanlines on 'mind' so they read as bloom, and give the hero monitor more content.
Keep the condensed type system and mono caps labels. Shrink MIND well below hero scale and let it glow only at its edges, so it is a lit word and not a green slab.
Keep the lit NOW line and the hatched idea swatches. Pull the ground back toward green-black and cut the blue grid and sheet furniture.
Keep the bronze and wood materials and the lamp-lit rows. Add real phosphor halo to the key word, the active tab and the progress traces so there is light in the page, not only on the monitor.

notes: The field splits between systems that changed the type (r20-mut-2, r20-mut-3, r19-mut-2) and systems that changed the material (r17, r18). The type-led ones answer the owner's 'reflect more of the page content' best, because the change shows on every heading and row. I put r20-mut-3 first because it alone keeps the phosphor light (halo, bloom, a lit rail) while moving to a new structure and type. r20-mut-2 is the most memorable but slightly loud. r19-mut-2 is the most elegant and the least Phosphor. The blueprint, patch-bay and pixel designs are distinctive but stray from the green-screen tube or readability.

scores.why: Coherent and recognisably phosphor. The halos and the tube are good, but the rest is stock rounded dark cards with one typeface. It is the yardstick for what the owner called nearly identical.

Condensed grotesque headings, a lit green MIND, a glowing rail with keyed section nodes, a perspective grid floor and a gauge with real bloom. It brings back the tube's light where attention belongs, and it carries across Home, Status, Plans, To do and Settings. It reads as one considered system with a clear console mood. It is a little busy in places.

The boldest typographic identity: a huge condensed MIND with a halo, a numbered ledger index, giant Settings entries and hatched kind swatches. It is memorable and clearly different from today on every page. The scale is slightly shouty on Home, and the tube is the only glass.

A warm serif display paired with the green gives the page real editorial taste. Creamy numerals, a track-diagram rail and the glowing dot-keys on filters are lovely. The halo on 'mind' stays, and the page is calm. The serif is less Phosphor than the condensed faces, and some pages are quieter.

Brass, wood and bronze trim, with patch cables on the heads and colour-coded cards. It is a distinct material world and the family would remark on it. The condensed caps are tasteful. It leans skeuomorphic, the halo is mostly gone, and Home below the fold was not rendered.

A blueprint sheet with a title block, a grid, scalloped bubbles and hatched swatches. It is vivid and fully committed, and it changes every page. But the teal-cream ground drifts from green-screen phosphor, and the grid and sheet furniture are heavy, so it is more drafting table than tube.

A pixel face, a NOW rail running down the page and a beige monitor bezel. It is playful and has a lovely retro charm. The pixel type costs readability, the bar-fill section heads look like placeholders, and the rail is a little gimmicky.

A polished dock layout with a left glass column, a tube that holds real data, lit rows and good list rhythm. It is tidy and well made but predictable, with little new personality in the type and colour.
A sound rework: the tube on the left, a numbered spine, a timeline of plans. It is clear but the closest to today in type and colour, so it risks the owner's 'nearly identical' verdict.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the condensed headings, the lit rail and the gauge bloom. Thin the grid floor and the bottom UP node so they do not compete, and give the Ideas head a bit more air before the tube.

Keep the ledger numbering, the hatched swatches and the glowing MIND. Drop the heading scale one step on Home and Settings so the type does not shout, and carry a little tube glow onto the other pages' key words.

Keep the serif and cream numerals and the dot-keyed filters. Restore a bit more phosphor glow on the key words of Status and To do, and make the track-diagram rail more consistent across Plans and Settings.
Keep the condensed caps and the bronze material. Put back some halo on the lit words, calm the cables to one per page, and check that Home below the fold holds up.
Keep the title-block heads and the hatching. Pull the ground back toward a green-black, lighten the grid, and keep the cream headline to the single lit word.
Keep the NOW rail and the beige bezel. Use the pixel face only for display sizes, replace the bar-fill heads with real labels, and set body text in a plain face.
Keep the dock and the data-bearing tube. Add one more distinctive typographic choice, a display face or numerals, and let the colour companions show on more of the page body.
Keep the timeline and the numbered spine. Give the headings a more distinct face and scale, and carry the colour and hatched kind marks further into the lists.

notes: The top three all change the page's content across every sheet (hierarchy, rails, type) instead of a corner, and carry the phosphor halo where attention belongs: the key word, the mark, the glass and the dial. r20-mut-3 wins as the most system-like. Its numbered sheet keys, rail and node, card grid and condensed display type repeat unchanged on Home, Status, Plans, To do and Settings. r20-mut-2 is the strongest typesetting but needs its hero tamed for comfort. r19-mut-2 has the best rows and controls but mixes too many faces. Material-heavy designs (Patch Bay, Blueprint, Green Desk) are coherent but decorative, and they trade legibility or the green-on-black identity for novelty.

scores.why: Coherent and comfortable, with the right tube glow on the monitors, but the page is a uniform stack of dark cards. Little hierarchy, one face, and the glass is the only thing with character.

The most complete system. Numbered keyed nav, a condensed display face with one lit word, a lit vertical rail with nodes, one card grid on Home, Status, Settings and Ideas, and a dial gauge on Status. Glow stays on the key word, the mark, the dial and the rail. Rows, rails and cards change on every page, not just the hero. Minor cost: lots of thin rail lines and some native-looking select styling.

The boldest typographic system: a huge condensed grotesque with mono labels, hard rules with coloured tabs, indexed A/B/C/D nav, and numbered Settings. It changes the whole page and reads as one language on every sheet. The oversized lit MIND? is glare for daily use, and the phone hero eats the viewport.

A rail and track-diagram idea carried through chat, To do and Status. A serif display face with counts, LED toggle chips and a styled open select are well judged. The serif, mono and sans mix is slightly eclectic, and the full-width neon Add button on To do and the pixelated MIND are loud.

A calm, tidy refinement: side dock plus main column, a desk-terminal glass with a Listening strip, even type steps, hairline ledgers and good controls. It is more of the existing page with better structure than a new system, so it risks the 'nearly identical' verdict, though the layout change is visible across pages.

A distinct material system (walnut bar, riveted plates, patch-cord rules, caps display face) applied consistently, with grounded brown and warm colours. It is skeuomorphic and heavy, the uppercase condensed titles are tiring, and the cards feel boxed-in. It holds on every page, but not as calmly.

A blueprint sheet system with title blocks, grid rulers and sheet numbers. It is coherent, but the teal grid ground drifts away from green on black, the background is busy, and the chat's scalloped bubbles are gimmicky. The tinted material is grounded but dilutes the phosphor identity.

The sound ancestor of mut-1: a terminal plus sections with numbered discs, tidy lists and a NOW timeline. Good bones and calm, but the least changed from today in the content area, and the later mutation does the same job better.

The pixel display face, hatched title bars, rail markers and tinted nav pills make a distinct system. Body legibility suffers from the pixel face and the dithered bars. Some chrome (ghost-bar headings, square rail nodes) is noisy and reads as decoration over function.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the keyed nav, the rail with NOW node, the dial, and the lit key word. Thin the rail lines where they cross dense cards. Style the Ideas Kind/Status selects like the other controls. Keep the Add button's glow at the Home Send level.

Keep the condensed display plus mono system and the coloured-tab rules. Cap the hero at about two thirds of its size, especially on the phone, and lower the bloom on MIND?. Keep the large-type page heads and the index numbering.

Keep the rail dots on To do and chat and the LED chips. Drop the full-width neon Add button to a standard primary button, and de-pixelate the Home MIND. Settle on two faces (serif display plus one sans) and let mono carry only data.

Keep the Listening glass and the dock layout. Add one stronger typographic move (a bigger section numeral or a display weight for page titles) so it reads differently from today on Plans, To do and Settings.

Keep the warm walnut/brass grounding and the patch-cord section rule. Cut the rivets and double-plate frames by half, set titles in sentence case, and give To do rows a lighter single line rather than boxed cards.
Keep the title block with sheet number and the ruler ticks. Lower the grid contrast on content areas, return the ground to nearer-black, and drop the scalloped bubbles for plain bordered ones.
Keep the NOW timeline and numbered section discs. Add a stronger type step for headings and a display numeral so the content differs more from today.
Keep the rail markers and square nav pills. Replace the pixel face with a readable sans for body and labels, keeping it only for the one lit word and numerals. Remove the dithered title bars.

notes: I judged from the cards only, because table.md and candidates-short.md were missing from the stage folder. The designs that win on comprehension give the eye one obvious first stop (the lit question), then the one action, then a numbered or ruled structure that carries across pages. r20-mut-2 does this most strongly and changes the pages visibly, which answers the owner's 'nearly identical' complaint. r20-mut-1 is the calmest and the safest. The weaker designs lose on legibility (pixel face, tiny caps) or on the phone's key control (the clipped textarea and the wrapped select in r19-mut-2).

scores.why: Calm and usable, with a clear composer and good focus rings, but the hierarchy is flat. Home is one big card, the eye has no strong first stop, and the sections look alike when squinted. The kind chips are small.

The squint read is clearest of all: a huge lit 'MIND?', then the field, then the green SEND, then a numbered index of sections. The change runs through every page (numbered tabs, big condensed names, ledger rules, hatch icons on ideas). Targets are generous and the focus rings are strong. Costs: the phone hero eats a lot of height, and the underline field is a weaker affordance.

The 'What's on your mind?' glass line with a Listening status gives the page an obvious entry point. On the phone it stacks the field, a full-width Send, the mic and chips well, and the dropdown is clear. The Ideas table (drive time, who it's for, number) is easy to scan. The page differs from today's mostly in Home and the list rows, so it reads as refined more than new.

A very clear sheet structure: a big cream title with a green key word, a title block with the page's one DO button, and numbered section heads. Numbered select options and double focus rings read well. The grid and the dashed chips add visual noise, and the scalloped user bubbles are a gimmick that makes the chat harder to read.

The keyed, numbered nav with icons, the rails and the section markers help orientation. The condensed headline is a good first stop and the buttons are clearly labelled. Rails, grid and markers run on every page, which makes it busy, and the phone's chips and hero are cramped.

The rail through the chat and To do turns the lists into a readable sequence. The serif page names with their counts give an honest glance read. On the phone the From select wraps onto two lines and the textarea is clipped to about two lines. That is a real comprehension flaw in the key control.

Joining Vera, the next-up readout and the question in one tube is a clear first stop, and the numbered sections below it are orderly. The phone shows a lot of tube before the Send button. The rest of the page is close to today's, so the difference from today is mostly in the corner.

The three-column Home shows everything at a glance, and the wood-and-rivet material is strongly different. Much of the text is tiny caps, the toggle and some buttons are small targets, and the chrome competes with the content. Low density of readable hierarchy for the family.

The pixel face makes headings and buttons slower to read, and the decorative placeholder bars in the headers carry no meaning. The left rail with its NOW marker is a good idea. The chat as a log is clear, and the full-width Send is a great target. The legibility cost keeps it last.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the huge lit question, the numbered index and the ledger rules. Cap the phone hero height so the Send button sits higher. Give the underline field a faint box or fill so it reads as a field.
Keep the glass question with the Listening line, the full-width Send and the Ideas table. Carry the table-rule and numbered-section treatment onto Plans and To do, so the change is not only on Home.

Keep the title block with the DO action, the numbered options and the cream headline. Replace the scalloped chat bubbles with plain ruled ones. Thin the grid behind the text, and fill the dashed chips so they read as buttons.
Keep the keyed nav numbers and the condensed headline. Remove some of the rail ornament, so each section gets one marker. Give the phone chips room, and balance the card grid on Ideas.
Keep the rail in the chat and To do, and the serif page names with counts. On the phone, shorten the From select's label so it stays on one line, and let the textarea show at least three lines.

Keep the joined tube and the numbered section heads. Shorten the phone tube so Send shows without scrolling. Push the lists further from today's with rules and a type step, so the change is not just the glass.
Keep the three-column density and the rivet material. Raise the smallest caps to 11px or more, enlarge the toggle and the task ticks to a 44px target, and use the wood on the bar only.

Keep the NOW rail and the full-width Send. Use the pixel face only for the one lit word and the big title. Remove the empty placeholder bars from the headers. Return body and button text to the sans face.

notes: Scored on the cards only: six close and home pairs read in detail and the rest skimmed, no full-size shots opened, and candidates-short.md missing at the given path. Today's type (00-current, about 5.5) is competent: a rounded sans, a mono for the glass, and a flat hierarchy where titles, section heads and body differ little. The strongest finalists change type across the page content: r20-mut-2 and r20-mut-3 with a condensed display face, tracked mono labels and numbered figures, and r19-mut-2 with a serif. The pixel-face design fights legibility, and the terminal and patch-bay designs are subtler.

scores.why: The most complete typographic overhaul. A condensed grotesque display face with a clear scale from giant MIND to page titles to tracked mono labels, numbered running heads and Ideas rows set as a ledger with big condensed titles. Changes run across Home, Chat and Ideas. The cost is that the MIND headline is large and glaring.

A condensed uppercase headline paired with tracked mono numerals and designators (00 HOME, 02, 12 IN ALL). A convincing system that holds on every page. Body and list text stay legible and the figures line up. The display type is more restrained than mut-2, so the hierarchy is a little flatter, and some small labels are tiny.

A high-contrast serif for titles, with large figures (Ideas 12, Status 6) paired with a clean sans and tracked small caps. It is the most elegant pairing and it differs from today across the page. Serif on phosphor is a slight stretch, and the glitchy 'mind' word is fussy at small size.

A wide extended caps headline in cream with a glowing MIND, tracked mono and caps labels, and sheet title blocks. It has a strong voice and good hierarchy. The wide caps get heavy at length, the small tracked labels are very small, and the grid chrome competes with the type.

Condensed tracked caps for titles and labels, with an LED-style date numeral in the list. Coherent and well scaled. Nearly everything is caps, which flattens the hierarchy, and the text throughout is small and dense.

A pixel-mono headline set on the glass and tidy tabular list columns. These are good, tasteful details but mostly an extension of today's type. The sans body and headings change little, so the family would see only a modest difference.
Mono headline in the terminal and tidy tabular columns with small caps column heads (FOR, #). Sound but close to today in the sizes and headings. The Home type is small and cramped.
A pixel face for titles and list item names (Chat messages, Who answers) hurts legibility and reads as a gimmick. The mixed faces lack a clear job each. The effect is bold but it fights readability.

Today's typesetting is clean and legible (a geometric sans for body and headings, mono for dates, labels and the monitor) but the hierarchy is flat and timid: one bold display size, a soft grey 12-13px body and tiny uppercase mono labels, with no real display or figure treatment, so it earns the baseline middle and sits below every candidate that added a stronger scale or structure.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the condensed display scale, the numbered ledger and the tracked mono labels. Cap the MIND headline size (about 70%) and tone its bloom so the type does not glare. Use tabular figures for the dates and set the body text a little larger.

Keep the system of numerals and tracked mono designators. Raise the 10-11px labels by a step and enlarge the page titles slightly for more contrast with body text. Keep tabular figures in the To do dues.
Keep the serif and big-figure pairing. Remove the glitch texture from 'mind' or limit it to one word. Make sure the serif's small sizes (the Who answers heads) keep enough weight.
Keep the cream extended headline with the lit MIND and the sheet blocks. Loosen the tracking on the wide caps, move the small labels up to 11px or more, and thin the grid lines behind the text.
Keep the condensed face and the LED date numerals. Use sentence case for item names, with caps only for labels, so the hierarchy opens up, and raise the small text sizes.
Keep the glass headline and the tabular columns. Add a real display step for page titles beyond the existing sans, and set section heads with a distinct tracked label style.
Keep the column heads and tabular figures. Enlarge the Home type, give the section heads a clearer scale, and add a more distinctive title style outside the monitor.
Confine the pixel face to the monitor and a few labels. Set titles and list items in a readable sans so the item names (Chat messages, Who answers) are legible.

notes: The stage markdown files (candidates-short.md and table.md) did not exist at the paths given, so I judged from the cards alone and did not see the measured contrast or target-size numbers. I scored on what a family does: write to Vera, spot what is late, find the add button, filter, and change a setting. The top three share clear primary actions, visible late-task state and consistent controls. They differ on phone Home polish and on how cryptic the nav is. The bottom three trade readability (pixel faces, small caps, grids, wood) for atmosphere. The current page is a competent baseline that mostly lacks at-a-glance state.

scores.why: Clear and predictable, with obvious primary buttons and labelled controls. It has weak overdue emphasis on To do and uniform cards, so you can't see at a glance what is late.

Easiest to use. The Home order is question, textarea, From, mic, big Send, ways to start. Each list page has a clear primary action top right (Add a task, Add a plan). Late tasks carry an amber 'was due 6 days ago' chip. Desktop nav is labelled (Memory, Family, Status, Settings) and the Settings sidebar means you never lose your place. The select has a check and a chevron. The monitor sidebar repeats a Ready line on every page.

Home is readable: a moderate headline, a full-width SEND, labelled From select and a clear checkbox. To do uses a dated rail with a 'now' marker and a green Add button, and the pills and search are obvious. Status and Settings are consistent card grids. Costs: tiny mono numbered nav ('03 PLANS') and a little grid noise.

Best state-at-a-glance. To do shows 'was due 6 days ago' on an amber rail, a full-width Add something to do button, and counts like '4 open, 3 late' and '9 parts, 1 needs a look'. Faults: on the phone Home the textarea is clipped (the placeholder is cut off) and the From select wraps onto two lines. The Plans clock dial adds nothing.

Solid and familiar. The late amber squares, NOW divider and labelled Show pills are good, and the 'On this page' index helps on Status. The terminal glass takes much of the phone's first screen before the composer, and the repeated Ready footer is noise.

Strong hierarchy and a clear Send. But the A/B/C/D and 00-05 nav letters are cryptic for a family. The huge condensed headline pushes the composer down. List/Month are bare text with no tab affordance. The select field has no visible chevron, and the Settings page is shouty.

The To do table with DONE, NO., TASK, WHO and DUE headers is genuinely clear. Sheet numbers like 'FD-09', a gridded background, thin dim cyan text and dashed buttons add clutter and lower legibility at night. Dashed ways-to-start read as less tappable.

The bright Send, filled active tab and amber active to-do tab are clear. The pixel-face headings and small pixel labels are harder to read, the timeline rail and double stripes are noise, and tiny type shrinks scanning on Settings and Status.

Small all-caps condensed labels everywhere, a brown wood bar, and low-contrast thin text in Plans cells and settings help text. Interactive controls are fine, but legibility on a phone at night is worst of the field.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the layout (monitor aside plus content), the labelled bar and the primary button top right. Drop the repeated Ready/Status footer from every aside, and make the Settings aside and list the same width so they don't repeat.
Keep the timeline To do and the Add button. Write the nav as 'Home, Vera' with the numbers dimmed, raise the tiny mono labels to at least 12px, and bring the Status section heads closer to the list.

Keep the due rail and the counts. On the phone, give the textarea a minimum height of about 4 lines and put the From select on one line (shorten its label or let it take the row). Drop the Plans clock dial or give it a job.
Shrink the phone terminal so the composer sits higher. Remove the Ready footer from every aside, and keep the NOW divider and the amber late squares.
Replace the A/B/C/D and 00-05 letters with plain words. Cut the headline height by roughly a third on the phone. Give List/Month a visible tab shape, and show a chevron on the select.
Keep the table headers on To do. Remove the sheet/FD numbers and lower the grid opacity. Lift the thin cyan text to at least 4.5:1, and make the ways to start solid-bordered.
Keep the full-width Send and the filled active tab. Use the pixel face only for the page title, not the card heads or labels, and remove the box-handle glyphs.
Set labels in sentence case at 12px or more instead of condensed caps. Lift the dim help text and the Plans cell text, and use a neutral bar instead of the wood one.

notes: The strongest finalists make the change visible in the content, not only in a corner. r20-mut-1 and r20-mut-3 do it with a glass dock and keyed page accents, and r19-mut-2 does it with figure-led titles and a rail, all while keeping the bright green to glass, mark and send. The weakest lean on a costume (cables, blueprint, pixels) that muddies the ground or hurts legibility. r20-mut-2 is the boldest typographically, but the giant glowing headline is the glare the owner asked to calm. Today's page is calm and bright where it should be, but it is nearly monochrome and its lists have little hierarchy.

scores.why: Calm, readable and the halo is real, but nearly one green on black. The cards, lists and settings are generic dark boxes with little hierarchy or companion colour, which is exactly the owner's complaint.

The question is typed on a lit glass, a gauge, scope or chart dock repeats on every page, and the green is bright only on glass, send and live dots. Lists get dotted leaders, amber late marks and a rail. The system shows across Status, Plans, To do and Settings. Weak spots: the dock takes a third of the width everywhere, and the Home hero is heavy.

Condensed headings, coloured numerals, a keyed accent per page and lit hairlines carry the change into content, and the tube light (halo, gauge, floor glow) stays on the glass. Weak spots: the faint grid and rail lines add clutter, and the teal tint on the ground edges toward an editor theme.

The serif display with counted figures, the track-diagram rail and the glowing key word make a fresh, calm pairing, and grounded companions sit well. The serif is not a CRT face, so some will say it loses the phosphor feel, and the green hero slab on To do is glare.

The most visible typographic overhaul, with huge condensed headings, ledger numbering and per-section colour bars, visible on every page. But the giant glowing MIND? is glare, the opposite of 'a little less bright and contrasty', and the headings shout over small mono captions.

A well-organised terminal-left layout with a numbered rail and lit scope, the earliest version of the dock idea. It is competent but plainer than its successor r20-mut-1: the dock appears only on some pages and the lists still read as stock rows.

Strong structure (sheet title blocks, ruled sections, a NOW trace), but the ground is a teal-grey blueprint costume with grid lines, scalloped chat bubbles and hatch swatches. It reads as a CAD theme, not a green tube, and the teal-tinged ground and grid lower the contrast.

The patch cables and screws are a costume, and the bronze/brown bar and frames are a muddy wash against the green. Spaced caps for every heading hurt readability. It has the most character but the least restraint.

The pixel face and dithered bars read as a retro game, and they cost legibility in dates and numbers. Solid-coloured pill tabs (green, blue, amber) are loud. There is little real phosphor light, and the left rail with its tick marks is noise.

fixes.suggestion: Keep the glass dock, the typed headline and the leader rows. Narrow the dock or let it collapse on short pages. Tone down the Home headline halo one step. Give the 'NOW' rail a little more companion colour in the Plans list.

Keep the keyed page accents and the condensed headings with coloured figures. Drop the grid and the perspective floor to a trace, neutralise the teal ground toward green-black, and keep bright green only on glass, mark and send.

Keep the figure-led titles and the rail with its lit now-node. Replace the full-width green Add button on To do with a normal-size primary. Consider a mono or slab alternative to the serif so it sits closer to the tube.
Keep the ledger index and colour bars. Cut the Home headline to about half its size and halve its glow, and keep the hero a size step below shouting. Lift the 10px caption sizes.
Keep the rail numbering and the scope. Carry the glass dock onto every page, as r20-mut-1 does, and give list rows a leader and an amber late mark.
Keep the title block and the NOW trace. Remove the grid, the scalloped bubbles and the hatches, move the ground back to a neutral green-black, and use the blue-teal only as a rule colour.
Keep the home's three-column cards with date plates. Drop the cables, screws and bronze wash, and set headings in sentence case.
Keep the Lately-added icon tiles and the tab-with-colour idea. Drop the pixel face for body and numbers, replace the dithered bars with plain rules, and make the pill tabs outlined rather than solid.
